Title: September 24, 2026 City of Boulder City Council Study Session
Overview: Council received a public safety update covering policing, police oversight, and the municipal court, with staff reporting on officer staffing, crime trends, the new public safety information center, and court outcomes for unhoused and young adult cases. Council then reviewed a preliminary framework to update the sister cities resolution, and members supported a council committee to oversee sister city relationships with staff to bring a formal resolution back at a future meeting.

Topic1.Title: Police Staffing and Retention
Topic1.Summary: Chief Redford reported authorization for 190 sworn officers with 12 vacancies and about 30 positions not deployable as solo officers due to recruits, academy, or injury leave. Dispatcher and records staffing were also discussed, with recruiting underway. Officer departures since 2021 and the young workforce were highlighted, with exit interviews citing cost of living, out-of-state opportunities, and the aging police building. Council asked what would help retain officers, and the chief cited union contract progress and public support.

Topic2.Title: Public Safety Information Center and Community Connect Cameras
Topic2.Summary: The chief introduced the new public safety information center, which consolidates technology and emergency monitoring and will be used for events and drone response. A council member asked how the voluntary Boulder Community Connect program lets residents share private camera feeds with police. The chief explained that feeds are viewed only when responding to calls, helping verify alarms and scale response. Privacy concerns were acknowledged, and the program was described as strictly opt-in.

Topic3.Title: Crime Trends and Proactive Policing
Topic3.Summary: Chief Redford reported decreases in property crime, including burglary, auto theft, and bike theft, and lower person crimes except assaults, which are rising. Proactive activity such as directed patrols, pedestrian contacts, and traffic stops is up compared with the three-year average while calls for service are down but more complex. Drug-related charges are up, especially downtown, and a bike theft study session is planned for October. Officers are also focusing on alcohol enforcement and underage drinking.

Topic4.Title: Significant Incidents, Assaults, and Overdoses
Topic4.Summary: Staff described a rise in financial crimes targeting vulnerable residents, with the Postal Inspector and other partners involved. Examples of serious assaults were presented, including an attempted murder case on Pearl Street where a drone helped locate the suspect. Officer assaults, including a choking incident that left an officer on injury leave, were discussed with credit to the District Attorney. Fatal overdoses, around 20 to 30 per year, were addressed through a drug task force case charging a dealer who supplied the fatal dose.

Topic5.Title: Community Engagement, Feedback, and Town Halls
Topic5.Summary: The chief described liaison groups for many community segments, Spanish-speaking outreach, and events such as an ice cream truck engagement and National Night Out. Post-contact surveys sent to over 6,500 people showed 85 percent satisfaction with police service. Police chief town halls were held in South, East, and downtown Boulder, with a North Boulder town hall scheduled and one requested for the hill. A monthly newsletter and public crime dashboards were promoted.

Topic6.Title: Council Questions on Drug Use, Care Team, and Data Requests
Topic6.Summary: Council asked about public drug use involving children and what can be done, and the chief noted state law changes that moved public drug possession from arrest to summons and jail limits. The high utilizers program and municipal court escalation were described as tools. Questions about the CARE team were answered by staff, who said the non-police response program lost a fire-based position and now operates with fewer clinicians. A council member requested race-disaggregated stop data and CARE outcome data, which staff agreed to provide.

Topic7.Title: E-Motos and Youth Traffic Safety
Topic7.Summary: A council member raised injuries to young people riding e-motos without helmets on bike paths and roads. Staff explained that many so-called e-bikes are legally motorcycles requiring plates and licenses, and that parents often buy them unaware. Education efforts include bike rack tags, bike shop outreach, and traffic unit enforcement, along with officers on e-bikes. Staff clarified that officers typically issue citations or provide education, with courts deciding accountability, and documentation is logged in the system.

Topic8.Title: Police Oversight Update and Five-Year Review
Topic8.Summary: Independent Police Monitor Sherri Dean and panel co-chairs reported on 2025 complaint data, including 149 allegations and 18 sustained findings, along with demographic trends and panel recruitment for the coming season. The co-chairs raised concerns that recent process changes have limited panel review to very few cases and reduced community complaint flow to the panel. A five-year review of the oversight system is underway with a consultant, and a report is expected in October with likely code changes. Council asked for data on officers who left in 2025 and whether they had complaints.

Topic9.Title: Municipal Court Presentation on Unhoused and Young Adult Cases
Topic9.Summary: Presiding Judge Jeff Khan explained that municipal court handles lower-level offenses, while felonies and more serious charges go to state court. He reviewed camping and obstructing government operations cases, community court dismissals, counseling sessions, and warrant and in-custody hearing trends. Young adult case data covered minor in possession, nuisance party, fireworks, and fraudulent ID charges, with outcomes like deferred prosecutions and restorative justice. Council members raised concerns about large amplified parties near CU and asked about enforcement consistency and comparisons with other case types.

Topic10.Title: Sister Cities Resolution and Process Update
Topic10.Summary: Assistant City Manager Pam Davis introduced a project to update Resolution 631 and clarify sister city application, review, reporting, and deactivation processes. The city clerk team reported on research from other cities, which found no dedicated staff or funding and identified needs for an online application, review timelines, and a deactivation process. Staff recommended five changes, and council supported a council committee of two members to oversee relationships, annual reporting, and possible cap or sunset criteria. Council gave non-binding direction, with staff to bring a revised resolution to a future meeting.
